name: The Earley Fig

location.address: Marengo Avenue at East Green Street, beside the Pasadena Convention Center, Pasadena, CA 91105

official_register.name: City of Pasadena Horticultural Landmark (designated 20 April 1971)

access: Free. Stands on the Marengo Avenue side of the Pasadena Convention Center grounds, visible from the public sidewalk.
transport: Metro A Line Memorial Park station, about 10 minutes on foot.
recognise: The big fig whose crown spreads over the corner of the Convention Center grounds at Marengo Avenue and Green Street.
verify_notes: Planted 1880 by Thomas Earley (PBS SoCal spells Early), Pasadena mayor 1907-1911, in front of his house at 170 S Marengo Ave; house gone, the tree stands over the Convention Center grounds. Pasadena board of directors designated it a Horticultural Landmark 1971 on Cultural Heritage Committee nomination (Pasadena Magazine 2016, PBS SoCal). Age 1880 planting is the sources' statement for this tree (no bridge). Alive: iNaturalist observation 337760549, genus Ficus, 2026-02-07, logged at Marengo Ave and E Green St (34.14453,-118.14602); the photo is CC BY-NC, not usable. The two articles likely share one origin, so flagged 'one source family'. Pin is the iNaturalist fix at the corner, not an identified crown, hence approximate. No measurements found on any fetched page.
story:
A future mayor of Pasadena planted this fig in his front yard in 1880. The house is long gone. The fig now spreads over the grounds of the Pasadena Convention Center.

The planter was Thomas Earley, by the account of Pasadena Magazine and PBS SoCal (which spells him Early), and the yard belonged to his house at 170 South Marengo Avenue. He served as mayor from 1907 to 1911, nearly three decades after the tree went in. That 1880 date is given for this tree itself, which puts it at about 145 years old and makes it one of the older figs on our Los Angeles list.

In 1971 Pasadena's board of directors named it a Horticultural Landmark, on the nomination of the city's Cultural Heritage Committee. A front-yard tree has since become a civic one, standing beside a convention centre where the Earley house used to be.

Two honest caveats. The two articles that tell this story probably go back to one shared origin, so read the details as one account rather than two independent ones. And nobody has published the tree's height or girth; if you know them, tell us.

It is free to see from the public sidewalk on Marengo Avenue. Our pin sits on the corner of Marengo and Green Street rather than on the trunk itself, which stands under the big crown on that corner of the grounds.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the big fig crown spreading over the corner of the Convention Center grounds. It stands on the Marengo Avenue side, near East Green Street.

name: Library Park Fig

location.address: South Pasadena Public Library, 1100 Oxley Street (west side), Library Park, South Pasadena, CA 91030

official_register.name: South Pasadena Historic Landmark Register, Landmark No. 55 (December 2018)

access: Free. Public park beside the library, open to everyone.
transport: Metro A Line South Pasadena station, about 8 minutes on foot.
recognise: The large fig on the west side of the library building.
verify_notes: Landmark No. 55 on the city's Historic Landmark Register, added by the city council December 2018. Planted by city street department worker Willem Kloezeman, 1930 per The South Pasadenan (a second South Pasadenan piece only says 'about 80 years ago' in 2011; one writer guessed 100 years, unverified). Younger than the Pasadena fig but a designated landmark. Alive: iNaturalist observations 133549102 (Ficus macrophylla, 2022-09-03) and 250170551 (2024-11-02) at Library Park, both CC BY-NC photos, not usable. Address 1100 Oxley St is the library's public address (not read on a fetched page; check). Pin is the iNaturalist fix in the park, the article places it west of the library. No dimensions published. One local-news source plus the city register: flagged.
story:
South Pasadena's Landmark No. 55 is not a house or a storefront. It is a fig planted by a man from the city's street department. The city council added the Moreton Bay fig beside the public library to its Historic Landmark Register in December 2018.

The South Pasadenan dates the planting to 1930, which would make the fig about 95 years old. The sources do not quite line up. A second piece in the same paper, from 2011, said only that it went in about 80 years earlier, which lands in the same years, while one writer guessed at a century without saying why. The 1930 date has the better footing.

That makes it a young tree by the standards of this page. The Earley fig in Pasadena, a few kilometres north, is half a century older. What the two share is a city's formal protection. This one stands in Library Park, a public park open to everyone, on the west side of the library building.

Nobody has published its height or girth. If you have measured it, tell us.

Access is free and there is no gate. The pin comes from a visitor's GPS record in the park rather than the trunk itself, so walk round to the west side of the library and look for the big fig there.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the large fig on the west side of the South Pasadena Public Library. It stands in Library Park, beside the library building.

name: Mission San Gabriel Olive

location.address: Mission San Gabriel Arcangel, 428 S Mission Drive, San Gabriel, CA 91776

access: Mission museum and gardens charge a small admission fee (listings disagree on the amount and hours; the church and gift shop are free). Closed on some holidays.
transport: Bus or car from Pasadena, about 25 minutes; the Mission is on Mission Drive in downtown San Gabriel (exact stop not verified).
recognise: The gnarled old olive beside the 'oldest olive tree and grapevine' sign, with the old grapevine nearby.
verify_notes: Waymarking transcribes the mission sign: olive tree and an old grapevine planted in the 1860s by Fr. Bot, one of the priests who looked after the mission from 1852 until the Claretians came in 1908; page calls it about 160 years old. Waymark coordinate 34.097117,-118.107083 (posted 2016); iNaturalist observation 172053880 (Olea, 2023-07-09) logged 34.09718,-118.10718, within about 10 m of that, so alive in 2023 and the pin agrees. The famous grapevine (a vine, reportedly c.1774 per a blog) is NOT delivered: the 1774 date is unsourced and it is a vine. Sign is on mission grounds, so confirmed pin but paid garden. One site source plus an independent observation: flagged. Admission figures not read on an official page (mission site returned 403); transport line is a rough bus estimate, writer should keep it generic.
story:
The sign in the garden of Mission San Gabriel calls this the oldest olive tree, and pairs it with an old grapevine. Both, it says, were planted in the 1860s by Father Bot, one of the priests who looked after the mission from 1852 until the Claretian order took over in 1908. That would make the olive about 160 years old.

So the olive was already some forty years old when the Claretians arrived, and has stood in this garden through all of their time here since. What you find is a gnarled old trunk in a garden court beside the church, which is a different kind of company from the figs in parking lots and convention centres elsewhere on this page.

It is worth being plain about the evidence. The planting date comes from the mission's own sign, as transcribed by a visitor, and from no other written source we could read. A visitor's GPS record from 2023 puts a living olive within about ten metres of that sign, so the tree is there and the pin agrees. The grapevine beside it is the more famous plant, with a much older date sometimes attached to it, but nobody has shown us where that date comes from.

The museum and gardens charge a small admission, and listings disagree on the amount and the hours, so check before you go. The church and gift shop are free.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the gnarled old olive beside the mission's 'oldest olive tree and grapevine' sign, with the old vine close by. It stands in the garden court.
